Infrastructure deployment: a fast-growing but uneven network

The worldwide network expanded strongly between 2016 and 2024, while regional deployment remained concentrated in a limited number of markets. The purpose of these charts is to show the trend—not to suggest that all stations offer the same capacity or availability.

How the chain works

A station works well only when supply and demand are balanced.

The source of hydrogen determines the equipment required on site. Delivered gas needs unloading and buffer storage; on-site production needs electricity, water treatment and maintenance capacity.

Design principle: size the station for real daily peaks and delivery constraints, not only for an annual average.

01

On-site production

Fewer road deliveries, but more utilities and equipment to operate.

02

Delivered hydrogen

Simpler production on site, with stronger logistics and storage needs.

03

Pipeline supply

Relevant for stable demand and sites connected to a wider network.

Risk control

Safety relies on several layers of protection.

Preventing a leak is not enough. Accumulation must also be limited, detected quickly, the installation isolated and an appropriate response prepared.

Risk scenario
ControlledTraining level
28 / 100Risk index
1
Prevent

Select compatible materials, limit ignition sources and monitor leak tightness.

2
Prevent accumulation

Ventilate high points and eliminate volumes where gas could remain trapped.

3
Detect and isolate

Sensors, automation and safety valves reduce response time.

4
Protect and respond

Separation distances, physical protection, procedures and training complete the design.

Barrier logic

From initiating event to controlled consequence

Safety is built as a sequence: prevent a release, stop accumulation, detect abnormal conditions and limit consequences.

PREVENTCompatible materialsLeak-tight designControlled venting
TOP EVENTUncontrolled H₂ release
PROTECTDetection + isolationVentilationEmergency response
Hydrogen behaviourRises rapidlyWide flammability rangeFlame can be difficult to seePressure stores mechanical energy
Low-visibility flame

Detection cannot rely on human observation alone: instrumentation and procedures are essential.

High pressure

Tanks, piping, fittings and safety devices must be designed, qualified and inspected for their intended service.

Operational safety

Safety must remain effective during normal use, maintenance and faults.

Technical barriers reduce risk, but they are not sufficient alone. Inspection, clear responsibilities and emergency procedures keep those barriers effective throughout the station life.

Practical focusMaintain access to valves, sensors and shutdown devices, and test them at planned intervals.

Before operation

✓ Verify leak-tightness

✓ Confirm ventilation paths

Directives and standards

The applicable framework depends on the equipment and site.

An installation may simultaneously be subject to rules on explosive atmospheres, pressure equipment, fuel quality, stations and national obligations. This page provides guidance, not an exhaustive regulatory assessment.

Explosion prevention

ATEX: identify and control hazardous areas

ATEX zoning identifies locations where an explosive atmosphere may occur and supports the selection of suitable equipment. Ventilation, detection, removal of ignition sources and documentation are part of the approach.

✓
Identify leak scenarios

Source, frequency, flow rate and potential duration.

✓
Define zones

Relevant volumes and ventilation conditions.

✓
Select equipment

Category, installation, inspection and maintenance.

Training note: the actual applicable framework must be confirmed by specialists according to the country, site, quantities, pressure and application.

A framework applied throughout the project lifecycle

Standards and directives do not replace engineering judgement. They organise responsibilities, performance requirements, verification and documentation from the first concept to decommissioning.

ConceptIdentify hazards, site constraints and intended use.
DesignSelect equipment, zones, materials and safety functions.
VerificationReview calculations, conformity and installation quality.
OperationControl procedures, competence, records and availability.
MaintenanceInspect, test, replace and manage modifications.
From rule to project decision

Compliance is built by combining several levels of requirements.

No single standard covers the whole project. The applicable set depends on equipment, pressure, location and national permitting.

Legal frameworkDefines mandatory obligations, authorisations and responsibilities.
Technical standardsProvide accepted methods for design, testing, quality and operation.
Site rulesTranslate requirements into procedures, inspections and records.

Good practice: create a compliance register early and update it whenever the design changes.

Understanding the business case

Utilisation is often more important than equipment price alone.

A station carries substantial fixed costs. When demand grows slowly, those costs are divided across too few kilograms. Oversizing can therefore be as damaging as undersizing.

FIXED COSTS

Paid even at low throughput

Site works, connection, engineering, core equipment and permits.

VARIABLE COSTS

Increase with operation

Electricity, deliveries, maintenance, consumables and staffing.

Forecast realistic demandStress-test low utilisationReserve room for expansion

Interpreting lifecycle results

The result changes with the boundary of the study.

Production is only one part of the footprint. Compression, cooling, transport and losses can materially change the final result.

Compare the same service

Use the same distance, payload or energy delivered.

State the electricity mix

Electrolysis impact depends mainly on the power source.

Include logistics

Distance and conditioning matter, especially for small volumes.

Future developments

Projects are moving from demonstrators to networks.

The next steps concern an ecosystem rather than a single technology: production capacity, large-scale storage, pipelines, terminals, committed users and common rules.

A possible pathway

Consolidate existing projects2026–2028

Improve electrolyser reliability, secure electricity contracts and increase utilisation of stations and hubs.

Connect ecosystems2028–2030

Deploy more interconnections, storage and multimodal corridors.

Industrialise value chains2030+

Standardise equipment, scale volumes and integrate hydrogen into energy and industrial networks.

2030 target

European targets are shaping infrastructure.

AFIR provides, by the end of 2030, for public stations with at least one tonne per day of capacity and a 700-bar dispenser, spaced no more than 200 km apart along the TEN-T core network, as well as at least one station in each urban node.

Backbone

New or repurposed pipelines connecting production and demand clusters.

Large-scale storage

Seasonal flexibility and security of supply.

Terminals

Import, conversion and distribution of hydrogen derivatives.

Hydrogen Valleys

Coordinated production and use at regional level.

E-fuels

Hydrogen used to produce synthetic fuels.

Skills

Training, maintenance, emergency response and engineering become critical.

Where infrastructure could expand next

Deployment is expected to focus first on corridors, ports, industrial clusters and territorial ecosystems where several users can share production, storage and distribution assets.

NetworksEuropean Hydrogen Backbone

Repurposed and new pipelines could link production areas, storage sites, ports and large industrial demand.

RegionsHydrogen Valleys

Local ecosystems combine several producers and users to share infrastructure and reduce demand risk.

MobilityHeavy-duty corridors

Stations for trucks and coaches need high availability, significant daily capacity and strategic locations.

IndustryIndustrial hubs

Steel, chemicals and refining can create concentrated demand that supports pipelines and large storage.

PortsImports and derivatives

Ammonia, methanol and other carriers may connect global supply with European consumption.

OperationsSkills and maintenance

Reliable deployment requires trained operators, emergency services, inspectors and maintenance teams.

What happens next?

Deployment will follow demand that is visible, concentrated and reliable.

New infrastructure is most credible when vehicles, industrial users, supply contracts and public planning develop together. Station counts alone do not show whether capacity is well used.

Near term

Fleet projects, local ecosystems and corridor stations create anchor demand.

Medium term

Interconnected hubs and shared logistics improve utilisation and resilience.

Long term

Pipeline backbones and imports may support larger industrial markets.

Final knowledge check

Seven questions verify the connections between the technical, regulatory, economic and environmental dimensions.

1. Which function absorbs differences between hydrogen supply and peak demand?

Buffer storage decouples supply from short-term demand peaks.

2. Which action directly limits hydrogen accumulation?

Ventilation at high points helps remove a very light gas.

3. What is the role of hydrogen detection in a safety system?

Detection reduces response time and supports automatic protective actions.

4. What is the main purpose of ISO 14687?

ISO 14687 specifies fuel-quality characteristics for hydrogen applications.

5. Why does utilisation strongly affect project cost?

Higher utilisation distributes capital and fixed operating costs over more hydrogen.

6. Which statement best describes lifecycle carbon assessment?

A lifecycle view accounts for the whole chain and clearly states the assumptions.

7. Why are hydrogen corridors and regional hubs important?

Corridors and hubs help aggregate demand and improve infrastructure utilisation.
